catalog_quote: Kikamba is a four-tone language in which the Super-High and Super-Low tone pattern together, thereby providing evidence that they share the tone feature [+extreme]. Moreover, this feature is sensitive to syntactic structure. Specifically, this feature must surface at the right edge of a maximal projection (X-Max). ... 5.2 The Kikamba tone system. Kikamba is a Bantu language with four tones: Super-Low (SL), Low (L), High (H), and Super-High (SH). In (5.1), we see that all four tones can be found on the surface in both nouns (5.1a-d) and verbs (5.1e-h).
sweep_summary: Two title-works with stress in the title, both already listed. (1) Philippson 1991 thesis: the catalog list of works to obtain had it as print-only, but the author's full PDF is open on the CNRS-DDL site (copied from the bemb1257 download, 542 pp. with text layer). Its Kamba section 3.12.1 (pp. 366-372) posits, alongside lexical H/L tone, an abstract penultimate demarcative accent realized only as L-register (plain L vs lowered L phrase-finally), never as length or intensity; Kamba remains 'pleinement tonale' (p. 253). Refines the tonal coding (Philippson's typology: tone + demarcative accent, like Chaga, unlike Kikuyu); it reinterprets Roberts-Kohno's Super-Low tone as post-accent lowering but does not supersede the 2000 dissertation. (2) Yukawa 1984 (already held by the project, first-hand Machakos data): 'accent' used as an umbrella term; Kamba accent 'basically pitch accent', two units H/L per segment, patterns multiplying with stem length; no stress posited; confirms tonal. Ford 1976 (held by the project, not a works with stress in the title) re-checked: tone only, silent on stress. No open stress-specific study of Kikamba exists in this search of works with stress in the title; nothing remains to acquire from these items. New files and are under The catalog record's entry in our list of works to obtain for Philippson (access 'print only') should be updated to open-and-held.

new_statements.quote: Le fait que l'opposition ne se maintienne que devant limites de groupe et ne concerne que la syllabe finale fait penser à un phénomène de type démarcatif. On peut interpréter les faits de la façon suivante : admettons que les mots kamba soient normalement affectés d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième, comme c'est le cas de nombreuses langues bantu à l'est de la Rift Valley. Cet accent ne peut se réaliser comme une longueur, ni même une modification de longueur, car le kamba connaît quatre degrés de longueur phonétique [...] et se réalise donc comme une modification du niveau des B.
new_statements.translation: The fact that the opposition is maintained only before group boundaries and concerns only the final syllable suggests a demarcative-type phenomenon. The facts can be interpreted as follows: let us assume that Kamba words normally carry a demarcative accent on the penultimate, as is the case in many Bantu languages east of the Rift Valley. This accent cannot be realized as length, nor even as a modification of length, since Kamba has four phonetic degrees of length [...] and so it is realized as a modification of the level of the L tones.
new_statements.citation: Philippson, Gérard. 1991. Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique Orientale: étude comparative typologique et diachronique. Thèse de Doctorat d'Etat, Université Paris V; NNT 1992PA05H011.
new_statements.locator: sec. 3.12.1.1, pp. 367-368 (printed = PDF page); cf. sec. 3.12 p. 366
new_statements.reading: Philippson keeps Kikamba a fully tonal language (p. 253) but adds, in the only explicit accent analysis of the language read in this search of works with stress in the title, that it also has a demarcative penultimate accent: an abstract accent whose sole exponent is the register of L tones before a pause (accented L higher than post-accent lowered L), neutralized inside prosodic groups, absent from monosyllables, never realized as length or intensity. This is the same phrase-final Low vs Super-Low contrast that Roberts-Kohno 2000 codes as a fourth tone at the right edge of X-Max. The statement is a comparative analysis built on Ford 1975/1976 and Whiteley 1963 data rather than Philippson's own fieldwork, and it posits an accent that would not count as word stress in the catalog's sense; it refines the 'tonal' coding (tone plus penultimate demarcative accent in Philippson's typology) without contradicting it.

new_statements.quote: On peut interpréter les faits de la façon suivante : admettons que les mots kamba soient normalement affectés d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième, comme c'est le cas de nombreuses langues bantu à l'est de la Rift Valley (cf. le chapitre suivant). Cet accent ne peut se réaliser comme une longueur, ni même une modification de longueur, car le kamba connaît quatre degrés de longueur phonétique [...] et se réalise donc comme une modification du niveau des B. Un B accentué est réalisé sur un registre plus élevé qu'un B situé après l'accent : les mots terminés par un B non-abaissé peuvent donc être considérés comme des mots (exceptionnellement) accentués sur la finale.
new_statements.translation: The facts can be interpreted as follows: let us assume that Kamba words normally carry a demarcative accent on the penultimate, as is the case in many Bantu languages east of the Rift Valley (cf. the next chapter). This accent cannot be realized as length, nor even as a modification of length, since Kamba has four degrees of phonetic length [...] and is therefore realized as a modification of the level of the L tones. An accented L is realized on a higher register than an L located after the accent: words ending in a non-lowered L can therefore be regarded as words (exceptionally) accented on the final.

new_statements.relation_note: Same work as the sole existing_statement; 367-368 (the earlier copy omitted '(cf. le chapitre suivant)' without an ellipsis) and adds the ch. 6 (p. 451) and Annexe (p. 513) formulations: Philippson keeps Kikamba tonal (catalog's classification, Roberts-Kohno 2000 four-tone) and refines it with a penultimate demarcative accent, partially free (penult default, final in a lexical minority and apparently in imperatives), whose only exponent is L-register / super-high pitch at the right edge of a prosodic group, never length or intensity. The 'four pitch levels' are the same phrase-final Low vs lowered-Low / H vs super-high contrast the catalog's four-tone analysis codes as tone. Not word stress…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kamba is 'une langue pleinement tonale' (p. 253) with lexical H/L tone on every syllable, and on top of it an abstract demarcative accent that falls by default on the penultimate syllable of the word; a minority of noun stems (Whiteley's counts: patterns b and d, about 14.5% of dissyllabic stems, mostly without Common Bantu equivalents, presumably loans, p. 451) are accented on the final instead. The accent has no length or intensity exponent; its only exponent is tonal: an L after the accent is realized as lowered L ('B abaissé'), a final H before it as super-high, giving four phonetic pitch levels at the end of a prosodic group (p. 365: 'le kamba et le chaga ont à la fois des tons et un accent démarcatif, qui interagissent pour produire quatre niveaux de hauteur distinctive'). The opposition exists only before a prosodic-group boundary (stratum 1) and only on the final syllable; group-internally it is neutralized (p. 366, p. 369). Annexe p. 513 sums it up: '3. : langue tonale, avec accent lexical partiellement libre' and '10. [statut de la syllabe pénultième] : néant'; p. 487: Kamba kept the Common Bantu tone oppositions 'mais y ont greffé un système accentuel à base pénultième'.
new_statements.exceptions: (a) Final-accented stems: 'les mots terminés par un B non-abaissé peuvent donc être considérés comme des mots (exceptionnellement) accentués sur la finale' (p. 368), fn 2 'La plupart d'entre eux n'a d'ailleurs pas d'équivalent en bantu commun'; p. 451: 'une opposition entre accent sur la pénultième et accent sur la finale.. Je n'ai pas d'explication à proposer sur l'origine de cette opposition, autre que l'emprunt des thèmes accentués sur la finale.' (b) Monosyllables show no accent opposition: 'l'opposition entre B "normal" et B "abaissé" n'est pas attestée dans ces mots.. Il n'y a pas de variation d'accent pour les thèmes se terminant par un H' (pp. 368-369). (c) p. 451 fn 1: 'Les impératifs semblent être accentués sur la finale, ce qui doit peut-être être mis en rapport avec des faits d'intonation'. (d) Neutralized inside prosodic groups: 'les mots placés à l'initiale du groupe ne peuvent plus s'opposer par leur accentuation' (p. 369). Data basis: Whiteley 1963 counts and Ford 1975/1976 transcriptions plus Philippson's own notes on Kamba (p. 515).
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson treats 'kamba' (groupe XXII, Kenya Central / Thagicu) as one language, built on Whiteley 1963, Ford 1975/1976 and his own notes (p. 515); no dialect is named. The comparison language in sec. 3.12.2 is Kikuyu, which he says lacks the accent difference in noun stems (p. 374), and in 3.12.3 Chaga (Vunjo dialect), which has a more elaborate version of the same accent system.

sources.note: First-hand (Machakos dialect, informant Paul Ndivo, fieldwork Nairobi 1980). 'Accent' is Yukawa's umbrella term; the substance is pitch, each CV/V/N segment of the stem is H or L, patterns multiply with stem length (up to 13 patterns for 4-segment stems), with a few length-independent alternating patterns (L-I, L-Ia, M) triggered by a following modifier. No stress, culminativity or fixed prominence position is claimed; the paper never uses 'stress' for Kamba itself. Tonal in the catalog's sense.
